CASE REPORT
Scleritis in a Person with Stiff-Person
Syndrome
Mehryar Taban,
Roger H. S. Langston,
and Careen Y. Lowder
Department of Ophthalmology,
Cole Eye Institute, Cleveland
Clinic, Cleveland, OH, USA
ABSTRACT Purpose: T o describe a case of anterior scleritis in a patient with
stiff-person syndrome. Methods: Case report. Results: A 55-year-old woman with
stable stiff-person syndrome and off immunomodulatory therapy developed
unilateral anterior scleritis, which resolved over three weeks with systemic non-
steroidal anti-inﬂammatory therapy. Conclusions: The authors are unaware of
reports regarding the association of scleritis with stiff-person syndrome.
KEYWORDS Stiff-person syndrome; stiff-man syndrome; scleritis
INTRODUCTION
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurologic disorder of middle age with
autoimmune features. It is characterized by progressive, severe rigidity or stiff-
ness of axial and proximal muscles superimposed by painful muscle spasms.
Simultaneous contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles are detectable by
EMG and relieved by benzodiazepines.
1
Formerly known as stiff-man syndrome, the female-to-male ratio is 2:1. SPS
was initially identiﬁed in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman,2 with further charac-
terization by Gordon et al. 3 in 1967 and by Lorish et al. 4 in 1989. The onset
of symptoms is typically insidious with spine and/or leg involvement seen in
all patients. The pattern of increased tone is caudal greater than rostral, unlike
tetanus.
1 There is a slow progression over months or years followed by long-
lasting stabilization. The stiffness may be either persistent or waxing and waning,
with the latter typically worsening during periods of stress.
1
The association of SPS with autoimmune disease is well known and con-
comitant autoimmune disease is found in most patients.5−7 Surprisingly, ocular
inﬂammatory ﬁndings have not been described in association with SPS. There
is only one reported case of immune-mediated retinopathy and one patient with
eye-movement abnormalities.
8,9 Herein, we describe a patient with anterior scle-
ritis and SPS.
CASE REPORT
A 55-year-old Caucasian woman with no signiﬁcant past medical history
other than for stable stiff-person syndrome complained of left eye pain and

cluded pseudophakia. Visual acuity was 20/20 in both
eyes. Pupils were equally reactive to light, without
a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pres-
sure was 16 mmHg in each eye. Extraocular motions
were full. Anterior segment examination was remark-
able for tenderness to palpation and deep episcle-
ral injection superiorly in the left eye (Fig. 1). The
rest of the ocular examination was normal. A diag-
nosis of anterior scleritis was made and the patient
was started on ibuprofen (600 mg 3 times a day).
FIGURE 1 (A, B) Anterior segment photograph of the left eye showing superior anterior scleritis.
The patient was followed over the following weeks.
The scleritis had resolved by the three-week follow-up
visit.
Laboratory evaluation to rule out a systemic cause
was performed and included normal complete blood
count, metabolic panel, syphilis testing, rheumatoid
factor, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, HLA-B27,
and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Chest radiography
was also within normal limits. Of note, patient had pre-
viously received systemic steroid and IVIg therapy for
sequelae of SPS.
M. Taban et al. 38

DISCUSSION
Autoimmune pathogenesis of SPS is suggested by
many factors. The presence of autoantibodies against
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) in 60–90% of pa-
tients suggests an autoimmune attack against GABAer-
gic inhibitory neurons.
5,10 GAD is the enzyme neces-
sary for the synthesis of GABA, an important inhibitory
neurotransmitter in the brain and spinal cord, and it is
localized in the presynaptic terminals of GABAergic
inhibitory synapses.
10 Two additional antibodies have
been subsequently implicated in paraneoplastic variants
of SPS: antiamphysin and antigephyrin.
11,12 Like GAD,
they are also involved in neurotransmission. Of note,
autoantibody levels against GAD do not correlate with
severity of disease or clinical course.
6 Hence, autoim-
munity against GAD may serve as a marker for hyper-
immune responsiveness, rather than being a primary
pathogenic agent.
Further support for the role of autoimmunity in SPS
comes from the high prevalence of at least one of a
number of autoimmune disorders including insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus, pernicious anemia, vi-
tiligo, sicca syndrome, Grave’s disease, Hashimoto’s
thyroiditis, myasthenia gravis, and autoimmune adrenal
failure in patients with SPS.
5−7 Moreover, immune-
suppressive treatment (steroids, IVIg) and plasmaphere-
sis have shown beneﬁt.
13,14 A front-loaded long-term
regimen of methylprednisolone (500 mg/day intra-
venously for 5 days followed by an oral regimen ta-
pering from 100 to 10 mg/day over 6 weeks) is rec-
ommended before IVIg therapy or plasmapheresis are
tried.
6
There are only rare ocular inﬂammatory ﬁndings de-
scribed in the literature and, to our knowledge, there is
no reported case of scleritis in SPS.
8,9 As stated earlier,
there is one reported case of autoimmune retinopathy
believed to be due to anti-GAD antibodies attacking
the inner and outer plexiform layers of the retina in a
patient with SPS.
8 Herein, we reported a case of anterior
scleritis in a patient with stable GAD(+) SPS. Although
one cannot attribute the anterior scleritis in our patient
to SPS with certainty, it is very plausible. Interestingly,
the sclera is embryonically derived from neural crest
cells.
